source_evidence.anchor: Remark 2.5.3, sentence beginning 'The constant 2 that appears'
source_evidence.observation: The remark explicitly says that the constant 2 appearing in some properties of Proposition 2.5.2 has no special meaning and may be replaced by any other absolute constant larger than 1.
Property (i) is the existence of K1 > 0 such that P{|X| >= t} <= 2 exp(-t^2/K1^2) for every t >= 0; its plain numerical prefactor is one occurrence addressed by the remark.
Property (iv) is the existence of K4 > 0 such that E exp(X^2/K4^2) <= 2; its right-hand-side threshold is the other plain numerical bound addressed by the remark.

source_evidence.anchor: Proposition 2.5.2 heading, 'the following properties are equivalent', and footnote 4
source_evidence.observation: The enclosing proposition asserts equivalence of properties (i)-(iv), with their positive parameters comparable up to an absolute constant factor; when E X = 0, property (v) joins the equivalence. Footnote 4 spells out parameter comparison as Kj <= C Ki for implications between properties.

binders: X is an arbitrary random variable, inherited from Proposition 2.5.2 (PDF page 13; printed page 24, proposition opening).
a is any fixed absolute numerical constant satisfying a > 1; the symbol a is analyst notation for the unnamed replacement constant in Remark 2.5.3 (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3).
K1, K2, K3, K4, and, in the centered case, K5 are positive scale parameters occurring existentially in the respective properties (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(i)-(v)).
hypotheses: The replacement value a is absolute and strictly larger than 1 (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3).

The claim is interpreted inside Proposition 2.5.2's existence-of-a-positive-parameter formulation, rather than with K1 or K4 fixed in advance (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(i) and (iv)).
If the equivalence is extended to property (v), the inherited assumption E X = 0 remains required (PDF page 13; printed page 24, sentence preceding property (v)).
conclusions: In property (i), the bound may use P{|X| >= t} <= a exp(-t^2/K1^2) for all t >= 0 in place of the displayed prefactor 2, without changing the sub-gaussian property characterized by Proposition 2.5.2 (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3, read with PDF page 13; printed page 24, property (i)).

In property (iv), the bound may use E exp(X^2/K4^2) <= a in place of the displayed threshold 2, without changing the sub-gaussian property characterized by Proposition 2.5.2 (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3, read with PDF page 13; printed page 24, property (iv)).

Thus the numerical choice 2 in those two bound positions is a normalization convention rather than an essential value; the equivalence is retained after allowing the positive scale parameters to change by absolute factors (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3, in the equivalence context stated on PDF page 13; printed page 24).
definitions_and_conventions: Property (i) is an existential tail estimate with K1 > 0 and universal range t >= 0: P{|X| >= t} <= 2 exp(-t^2/K1^2) (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(i)).
Property (iv) is an existential exponential-square moment estimate at one scale K4 > 0: E exp(X^2/K4^2) <= 2 (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(iv)).

The proposition's phrase 'differ ... by at most an absolute constant factor' is made precise in footnote 4 by an absolute C satisfying Kj <= C Ki for the implication from property i to property j (PDF page 13; printed page 24, footnote 4).

The phrase 'constant 2' in the remark concerns the plain bound constants in properties (i) and (iv), not the exponent 2 in squares such as X^2, lambda^2, or Ki^2; this is a structural reading of the displayed properties (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(i)-(v), and PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3).
implicit_context: For every random variable X, properties (i)-(iv) are equivalent (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2 opening and first 'Moreover' sentence).
For centered X, meaning E X = 0, property (v), the all-real-lambda MGF estimate for X, is also equivalent to properties (i)-(iv) (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(v)).
Remark 2.5.3 is a claim to be checked and does not supply its own proof (PDF page 15; printed page 26, terminal parenthetical '(Check!)').

details: The replacement constant is universally selectable among fixed absolute values a > 1, while K1 or K4 remains existential for the corresponding property (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3, together with PDF page 13; printed page 24, properties (i) and (iv)).
The tail inequality keeps its original universal quantifier over all t >= 0 (PDF page 13; printed page 24, property (i)).

The semantic content is invariance of the sub-gaussian characterization under changing the two displayed normalization bounds from 2 to an arbitrary fixed absolute value greater than 1 (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3).

The claim is not literal invariance with the same numerical K1 or K4; the enclosing proposition treats each property through existence of its own positive parameter and compares parameters only up to absolute factors (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2 and footnote 4).

Changing the normalization constants in properties (i) and (iv) does not remove the separate centering hypothesis required to include property (v) in the equivalence (PDF page 13; printed page 24, 'Moreover, if E X = 0').

undebatable_constraints: The replacement value must be an absolute constant strictly larger than 1 (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3).

The replaceable plain bound constants are the tail prefactor in property (i) and the right-hand-side exponential-moment threshold in property (iv) (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2(i) and (iv), read with PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3).

Squares and power indices denoted by 2 are not replacement targets (PDF page 13; printed page 24, the structural distinction between the plain constants in (i)/(iv) and exponent occurrences throughout (i)-(v)).

All original quantifiers and side conditions remain: t ranges over every t >= 0 in (i), each Ki is positive and existential, and E X = 0 is still needed for the equivalence with (v) (PDF page 13; printed page 24, Proposition 2.5.2).

The claim concerns equivalence after permissible rescaling of parameters up to absolute factors, not equality of optimal K-values under different normalization constants (PDF page 13; printed page 24, proposition heading and footnote 4; PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3).

ambiguities.issue: The remark does not say whether the two occurrences must be replaced simultaneously by one common value, may be replaced independently by two values, or both.
ambiguities.evidence: Remark 2.5.3 uses the singular wording 'The constant 2 ... it can be replaced' while properties (i) and (iv) contain two distinct bound occurrences (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3; PDF page 13; printed page 24, properties (i) and (iv)).
ambiguities.impact: The unambiguous core is that each displayed choice of 2 is inessential. A formal statement demanding simultaneous use of one shared replacement constant is a defensible specialization, but independent replacement is not explicitly stated.

ambiguities.issue: The source does not quantify how the parameter-comparison factor depends on the chosen replacement constant, especially as that constant approaches 1.
ambiguities.evidence: The remark only requires an 'absolute constant ... larger than 1'; Proposition 2.5.2 and footnote 4 assert comparison up to an absolute factor but give no replacement-dependent formula (PDF page 15; printed page 26, Remark 2.5.3; PDF page 13; printed page 24, footnote 4).
ambiguities.impact: The source supports equivalence for each fixed absolute replacement value, but it does not explicitly assert one comparison factor uniform over all choices a > 1.

ambiguities.issue: The remark does not explicitly state a downstream reformulation of the sub-gaussian norm, which is later normalized using the threshold 2.
ambiguities.evidence: Remark 2.5.3 refers specifically to 'properties in Proposition 2.5.2' (PDF page 15; printed page 26), while Definition 2.5.6 later defines the norm using E exp(X^2/t^2) <= 2 (PDF page 16; printed page 27).
ambiguities.impact: An equivalent norm based on another threshold greater than 1 is a natural consequence to establish separately, but it is not included as an explicit conclusion of the selected remark.

contract_plain_english: Remark 2.5.3 says that the number 2 used as the front constant in the tail bound of Proposition 2.5.2(i) and as the threshold in the exponential-square moment bound of Proposition 2.5.2(iv) is only a normalization choice. Either bound can instead be formulated with any fixed universal numerical constant greater than 1, after allowing its positive scale parameter to change by an absolute factor, and the same sub-gaussian characterization results. The original quantifiers and the mean-zero assumption needed for property (v) are unchanged. The source does not specify whether the two replacements must share one value or how comparison factors behave uniformly as the replacement value tends to 1.
